summary: Year 5 pupils move from counting squares to applying area = length × width and perimeter = 2 × (length + width) for rectangles (including squares), used both forwards and to find a missing side, with area labelled in square units (cm², m²) and perimeter in linear units (cm, m). They also estimate the area of irregular shapes on a cm² grid by counting whole and part squares, treating the result as an estimate. The central risk is instrumental learning that confuses area and perimeter or reports area in linear units; the antidote is keeping each formula anchored to meaning — area as unit squares covering the surface, perimeter as distance around the edge. Activities below range from a hands-on/grid manipulation intended to make the two quantities visibly distinct, through a tap-to-reveal formula scaffold, to a checking quiz, each with its own purpose and limits.
misconceptions: Confuses area and perimeter — uses one formula for the other, or gives the distance around when asked for the covered surface.
Overgeneralises 'area = length × breadth' and reports the answer in linear units (cm) instead of square units (cm²).
When estimating irregular area, counts only whole squares and ignores part-squares (or counts every touched square as a whole).

activities.title: Grid playground: reshape a rectangle and watch area and perimeter move apart
steps: On cm² paper (physical squared paper or an on-screen grid), draw or drag the corners of a rectangle and, as it changes shape, keep two counts — tallied by hand on paper or shown live on screen: the squares filling the inside (area, in cm²) and the units traced around the outline (perimeter, in cm).
Compare a 6×4 rectangle (24 cm², 20 cm) with other shapes you make, saying aloud which count is 'squares covering it' (area) and which is 'steps around it' (perimeter).
Switch to a 'missing side' task: with the area fixed at 48 cm² and the length given as 8 cm, find the width (6 cm); then try area 48 m² with length 8 m → width 6 m.
Switch to an 'irregular blob/pond' task: shade whole squares and part-squares on the grid and combine them to estimate the blob's area, stating that it is an estimate.
activities.insight: Area and perimeter are different quantities with different units: area counts the unit squares covering a surface (cm²); perimeter measures the distance around the edge (cm). One can stay the same while the other changes as a shape is reshaped.

activities.title: Build l × w from an array of unit squares, then express a missing side algebraically
steps: Cover a labelled rectangle with unit-square tiles (or draw the array on squared paper) and count the squares by rows × columns to see where length × width comes from.
Compute the perimeter of the same rectangle as 2 × (length + width), and label each answer with its unit (cm² for area, cm for perimeter).
Find a missing dimension: given area 48 m² and length 8 m, work back to width 6 m; calculate the area of a square with side 7.5 cm (56.25 cm²).
Write a missing-measure problem as an equation, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20, and solve for b.
activities.insight: The area formula is a shortcut for counting rows × columns of unit squares, and a missing side can be found by reasoning backwards from the area (or as an equation), while perimeter adds the edge lengths.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal formula reference (scaffold)
steps: On a static labelled rectangle, tap the length and width to reveal l × w (area) and 2 × (length + width) (perimeter).
Note the unit each answer takes — cm² for area, cm for perimeter — and say why they differ.
activities.insight: Recall the two formulae and the correct unit for each as a memory and reference aid.

activities.title: Checking quiz: area, perimeter, missing side and estimate with a units check
steps: Compute the area and the perimeter of a labelled rectangle, then answer a units question (is the area cm or cm²?).
Find a missing width when given the area and the length.
Estimate the area of a gridded blob, including part-squares.
activities.insight: Confirm that the learner can apply both formulae accurately, choose correct units, and estimate an irregular area.

checkQuestion: Give the child a rectangle labelled 8 cm by 3 cm drawn on cm² paper and, on the same grid, an irregular blob. Say: 'Find the area of the rectangle, then its perimeter, then estimate the area of the blob — and label each answer with its units.' Then WATCH: which operation they use for each, whether they keep area and perimeter distinct, whether area is cm² and perimeter cm, and how they treat the blob's part-squares.
checkAnswer: Computes area 24 cm² (8×3) and perimeter 22 cm (2×(8+3)), keeps the two distinct with correct units, and estimates the blob's area by counting whole squares plus part-squares (roughly counting halves), presenting it as an estimate.
